SUBJECT: EVALUATION OF TRAFFIC SPEEDS ON SHERWOOD ROAD
  BETWEEN OLD MILL ROAD AND ST ALBANS ROAD

STRATEGIC PLAN CRITICAL SUCCESS FACTORS

Safe Community
Well-Maintained Infrastructure

BACKGROUND

Staff were contacted by residents regarding concerns of vehicular speeding on
Sherwood Road between Old Mill Road and St. Albans and requested the City
to evaluate potential ways to reduce speeding. Based upon the resident’s
concerns, staff initiated a review of the vehicular speeds and traffic collision
history. The Traffic Engineers of Hartzog & Crabill Inc. (HCI), one of the City’s
on-call traffic engineers, completed the attached August 28, 2025, evaluation
of traffic speeds on Sherwood Road Road. In addition to analyzing vehicle
speeds and collision history, HCI also performed a field review of the roadway.
Their analysis includes recommendations based on an incremental approach
to potential improvements.

DISCUSSION

As the basis of their evaluation, HCI coordinated the collection of 24-hour
Average Daily Traffic (ADT) counts, including speed data, over five separate
days (3 weekdays and 2 weekend) in order to obtain both weekday and
weekend data. The speed survey determined the 85th percentile speeds on
Sherwood Road range between 30 to 34 MPH with average speeds ranging
from 23 to 26 MPH. A full table containing all speed data is included on page
13 of Attachment 1. A 5-year traffic collision history review was also included

  PAGE 5 of 103
 in the study which determined one traffic collision had been reported during
this time and was noted as not speed related.

Based on HCI’s evaluation, the 85th percentile speeds were within the typical
prevailing speed range for similar streets without traffic safety concerns and
the limited number of collisions in the area indicates that hardscape
improvements to lower travel speeds are not warranted. Additional driver
education through the deployment of the speed radar trailer and additional
enforcement as resources permit is recommended to address the speed of the
small percentage of drivers exceeding the 85th percentile speed. HCI’s report
also includes multiple recommendations for the location that can incrementally
improve traffic/pedestrian safety (found on page 11 of Attachment 1),
including:

Initial Steps
1. Increase law enforcement presence as resources permit
2. Place portable radar speed trailer near the midpoint of the roadway
segment, as often as available.
3.Consider installation of ‘25’ pavement markings at the speed limit sign
locations.
4. Consider installation of a Stop sign, Stop marking, and limit line on
Sherwood Road facing its eastbound approach to St Albans Road.

Follow Up Steps
1. Consider installation of white right-edgeline stripe on both sides of the
roadway along the entire segment, narrowing the two travel lanes to
potentially reduce travel speeds.

Staff has reviewed and supports HCI’s recommendations for an incremental
approach and recommends beginning with the initial steps for improvements
on Sherwood Road. Staff recommend the Public Safety Commission review
and approve the recommended improvements as proposed by HCI. The next
step will be for staff to begin implementation of the improvements.

BACKGROUND

Sherwood Road, from Old Mill Road/Lorain Road easterly to St Albans Road, is a
diagonal east-west, local roadway with single-family residential properties on either side
of the street. The roadway is approximately 48 feet wide curb-to-curb, and has concrete
curb, gutter, parkway, and sidewalk improvements on both sides. There are also several
10-foot decorative street lights staggered along both sides of the roadway.

The 2-lane roadway provides for one lane of traffic in each direction, separated by yellow
centerline striping.

On-street parking is allowed on both sides of the street.

Sherwood Road has a speed limit of 25 MPH, via signs posted at each end of roadway
segment.

The roadway also has two Neighborhood Watch signs posted on each end.

At the westerly end of the evaluation segment, there is a 4-Way Stop sign installation at the
intersection with Old Mill Road/Lorain Road.

At the easterly end of the segment, which is a T-intersection at St Albans Road, there are no
existing Stop signs (i.e., uncontrolled on all three approaches).

24-hour Vehicular Speed Counts

counts, which included vehicular speed data, were taken using a machine counter and
road tubes at a midpoint location of Sherwood Road, between Old Mill Road and St
Albans Road. The location was chosen to obtain the most ‘free flow’ traffic speeds
between the evaluation limits. The vehicular traffic data was collected on three weekdays
and two weekend days (i.e., Wednesday - Sunday), in order to provide average vehicular
speeds occurring during the week and weekend, with results summarized below:

SUMMARY OF RESULTS & FINDINGS

    At the westerly end of the evaluation segment, there is a 4-Way Stop sign
  installation at the intersection with Old Mill Road/Lorain Road.

    At the easterly end of the segment, which is a T-intersection at St Albans Road, there
  are no existing Stop signs (i.e., uncontrolled on all three approaches).

    Roadway striping along Sherwood Road, between Old Mill Road and St Albans
  Road, primarily consists of a yellow skip-center line stripe along the entire
  segment, including a double-yellow centerline stripe at the limits.

    (Qty. 2) Neighborhood Watch signs posted at each end of the segment.

    (Qty. 2) 25 MPH Speed Limit signs posted at each end of the segment.

    5-Day, 24-hour Speed-Count results for segment, from Old Mill Road to St
  Albans Road,  Average = 25 MPH; 85th-Percentile = 33 MPH. The 85th
  percentile speed is 8 MPH above the 25 MPH posted speed limit, which is
  generally expected and considered in typical range for this type of roadway.

    Collision Data Results = One (1) collision reported along this segment of
  Sherwood Road in the past five+ years, which was not categorized as speed-
  related.

RECOMMENDATIONS

Based on the roadway collision history alone, there is no indication to support the
implementation of hardscape improvements on this segment of Sherwood Road.

However, since the 85th-percentile speeds were verified as higher than the local 25 MPH
speed limit (but considered within typical range for this type of roadway), an incremental
approach is suggested below for the City’s consideration in addressing travel speeds on
this roadway.

Initial and follow-up steps include:

1st Steps:
   Increase law enforcement presence as often as available, or as resources permit.
   Place a portable radar speed trailer near the midpoint of the roadway segment, as
  often as available.
   Consider installing new 25 MPH speed limit signs at more visible locations.
   Consider installation of ‘25’ pavement markings at the speed limit sign locations.
   Consider installation of a Stop sign, Stop marking, and limit line on Sherwood
  Road facing its eastbound approach to St Albans Road (please see Appendix C
  showing an exhibit of the above considerations).

2nd Steps:
   In conjunction with the existing centerline striping, consider installation of a
  white right-edgeline stripe on both sides of the roadway along the entire segment,
  narrowing the two travel lanes to potentially reduce travel speeds.
   Conduct a community meeting to help make all residents aware of speeding.

BACKGROUND

In response to concerns raised by residents and members of the Public Safety
Commission, staff initiated a review of the vehicular speeds, roadway width,
and visibility on Virginia Rd between Oak Grove Avenue and Rosalind Rd. The
Traffic Engineers of Hartzog & Crabill Inc. (HCI), one of the City’s on-call traffic
engineers, completed the attached August 29, 2025, evaluation of Virginia
Road. In addition to analyzing vehicle speeds and collision history, HCI also
performed a field review of the roadway, including an analysis of roadway
width and visibility. Their analysis includes recommendations based on an
incremental approach to potential improvements.

DISCUSSION

As the basis of their evaluation, HCI coordinated the collection of 24-hour
Average Daily Traffic (ADT) counts, including speed data, over five separate
days (3 weekdays and 2 weekend) in order to obtain both weekday and
weekend data. The speed survey determined the 85th percentile speeds on
Virginia Road range between 32 to 37 MPH northbound and between 32 to 34
MPH southbound, with average speeds ranging from 28 to 32 MPH
northbound and 27 to 29 MPH southboound. A full table containing all speed
data is included on page 13 of Attachment 1. A 5-year traffic collision history

  PAGE 29 of 103
 review was also included in the study which determined two traffic collisions
had been reported during this time but were noted not to be speed related.

Based on HCI’s evaluation, the 85th percentile speeds were within the typical
prevailing speed range for similar streets without traffic safety concerns and
the limited number of collisions in the area indicates that hardscape
improvements to lower travel speeds are not warranted. Additional driver
education through the deployment of the speed radar trailer and additional
enforcement as resources permit is recommended to address the speed small
percentage of drivers exceeding the 85th percentile speed. HCI’s report also
includes multiple recommendations for the location that can incrementally
improve traffic/pedestrian safety (found on page 11 of Attachment 1),
including:

Initial Steps (see Appendix D for exhibit)
1. Increase law enforcement presence as resources permit
2. Place portable radar speed trailer near the midpoint of the roadway
segment, as often as available.
3.Install a Curve Ahead warning sign to accompany the existing 20 MPH
supplemental placard that faces northbound traffic.
4. Consider relocation of the existing speed limit signs to more noticeable
locations.
5. Consider installation of a Stop Ahead warning sign, including pavement
markings, to face the northbound approach in advance of Oak Grove Avenue.
6. Consider offsetting the existing centerline striping easterly by
approximately three (3) feet to achieve an 18-foot wide southbound lane and
a 12-foot wide northbound lane, since on-street parking is prohibited along
the entire east-side of the roadway.

Follow Up Steps
1. Consider installation of white right-edgeline stripe on the west side adjacent
to the on-street parking lane along the entire segment, essentially narrowing
the southbound travel lane to potentially reduce travel speeds.

Staff has reviewed and supports HCI’s recommendations for an incremental
approach and recommends beginning with the initial steps for improvements
on Virginia Road. Staff recommend the Public Safety Commission review and
approve the recommended improvements as proposed by HCI. The next step
will be for staff to begin implementation of the improvements.

The 2-lane roadway provides for one lane of traffic in each direction, which are separated
by single-yellow skip centerline striping within the segment, and double-yellow
centerline striping at the evaluation limits.

On-street parking is allowed only on the west-side of the roadway. On-street parking is
prohibited on the east-side via several posted No Parking Any Time – Tow Away signs,
including a couple of small sections of red curb.

Virginia Road has 25 MPH Speed Limit signs posted on each side of the roadway.

Roadway Width

As mentioned, Virginia Road is a 2-lane roadway with a 30-foot curb-to-curb width.

The two opposing lanes are separated by single-yellow skip centerline striping within the
segment, and double-yellow centerline striping at the evaluation limits.

On each side of the centerline stripe is a 15-foot wide southbound lane and a 15-foot wide
northbound lane.

As also mentioned, on-street parking is allowed only on the west-side of the roadway.

The width of the unmarked parking lane along the west-side is generally 8 feet wide from
curb face.

So when vehicles park along the west-side that leaves only 7 feet for the southbound
through lane, which is considered too narrow.

Since on-street parking is prohibited along the entire east-side of the roadway, it would
be appropriate to offset the centerline striping easterly by approximately 3 feet (i.e., to
achieve an 18-foot wide southbound lane with on-street parking allowed, and a 12-foot

Visibility

Impaired visibility, or restricted sight distance, due to the geometry of the two T-
intersections located ‘within’ the project limits (i.e., Canon Drive and Encino Drive) were
carefully considered during our field-review of the surrounding residential neighborhood
property environment. The geometry of the two intersections includes an approximate
90° angle, which is favorable for side-street sight distance. Virginia Road and Canon
Drive have a consistent, slightly gradual incline towards the northbound direction, while
Encino Drive has a slight, gradual decline towards as you proceed in the south direction.

Driver sight distance was measured from both side-street approaches, as traffic on these
approaches are required to stop and look both ways before proceeding to make a left-turn
or right-turn onto Virginia Road. The measured distance was derived from the stopping
sight distance guidelines found in the California MUTCD (see Appendix C). In this
reference, a 25 MPH roadway speed recommends a minimum Stopping Sight Distance of
155 feet. However, it has been shown that the 85th percentile speeds exceeded the 25
MPH posted speed limit. Therefore, a 35 MPH roadway speed was used as a more
conservative measure, which has a minimum sight distance of 250 feet. This distance
was used when looking towards approaching, uncontrolled traffic along Virginia Road.
More specifically, this stopping sight distance was field-measured from a typical
‘stopped’ vehicle location at the side-streets looking towards the oncoming lanes of
cross-traffic along Virginia Road. An orange cone was placed at this distance and a
photograph was taken from a stopped driver’s perspective (i.e., approximately 3.5 feet in
height). (See sight distance photos in Exhibits 5 & 6 on the following pages).

As Exhibits 5 & 6 show, when looking from the two side-streets, a driver does have a
clear line-of-sight towards 250 feet when looking both ways on Virginia Road.

RECOMMENDATIONS

Based on the roadway collision history alone over the past five (5+) years, there is no
indication to support the implementation of hardscape improvements on this segment of
Virginia Road.

However, since the 85th-percentile speeds were verified as higher than the local 25 MPH
speed limit (but still considered within typical range for this type of roadway), an
incremental approach is suggested below for the City’s consideration in addressing travel
speeds on this roadway. It is important to note, these are suggestions only and not
considered mandated recommendations. Initial and follow-up steps include:

1st Steps:
   Increase law enforcement presence as often as available, or as resources permit.
   Place a portable radar speed trailer near the midpoint of the roadway segment, as
  often as available.
   Install a Curve Ahead warning sign to accompany the existing 20 MPH
  supplemental placard that faces northbound traffic (appears to be missing).
   Consider relocating the existing speed limit signs to more noticeable locations.
   Consider installation of new 25 MPH Speed Limit signs at the roadway limits,
  including ‘25’ pavement markings.
   Consider installation of a Stop Ahead warning sign, including pavement
  markings, to face the northbound approach in advance of Oak Grove Avenue.
   Consider offsetting the existing centerline striping easterly by approximately three
  (3) feet to achieve an 18-foot wide southbound lane and a 12-foot wide
  northbound lane, since on-street parking is prohibited along the entire east-side of
  the roadway.
   Please see Appendix D showing an exhibit of the above considerations.

2nd Steps:
   In conjunction with the proposed centerline striping, consider installation of a
  white right-edgeline stripe on the west-side adjacent to the on-street parking lane
  along the entire segment, essentially narrowing the southbound travel lane to
  potentially reduce travel speeds.
   Conduct a community meeting to help make all residents aware of speeding.

BACKGROUND

The San Marino Fire Department completes a monthly report for the Public
Safety Commission, providing an overview of department activities, significant
incidents, and monthly statistics.

DISCUSSION

During the month of June, the Fire Department conducted interviews for the
position of Firefighter/Paramedic. The Fire Department received a total of 19
applications for two vacancies at the Firefighter/Paramedic rank. A total of
eight candidates were invited for interviews and a paramedic assessment
evaluation. The top two candidates completed the criminal background
investigation and physical fitness examination process and participated in a
week-long orientation training program during the week of August 25. One
candidate unfortunately resigned following the completion of his orientation.
FF/PM Austin Previch successfully completed his orientation on August 28 and
began shift rotation on August 29. There is currently one vacant position at
the FF/PM rank; additionally, there is one vacancy at the Captain position due
to a long term, duty connected injury that is being filled by acting personnel.

  PAGE 65 of 103
 The Fire Department is also in the process of conducting a promotional
examination for the position of Division Chief. Division Chief Eric Zanteson
retired from the South Pasadena Fire Department in June 2025, creating a
vacancy in the Division Chief position shared by both departments. The
promotional examination is scheduled for Monday, September 15 through
Wednesday, September 17.

On Sunday, August 18, Firefighter James Jarboe successfully passed his
twelve-month probationary examination. The exam included a variety of
practical life-saving, rescue, and firefighting skills, and both firefighting and
paramedic written examinations. Firefighter Jarboe will be assigned a special
project to be completed by the end of his 18-month probationary period.
Congratulations Firefighter Jarboe!

South Pasadena Agreement
On September 10, the City Council approved an updated agreement with the
City of South Pasadena for shared command services. The revised agreement
provides clear guidance for how shared costs are calculated and reimbursed,
including salary, training, benefits, backfill coverage, and command vehicle
expenses. It also updates the position’s roles and responsibilities, and
restructures command vehicle lease payments to an annual schedule, rather
than quarterly.

Fire Code
On September 10, the City Council took the first step to adopting the 2025
California Building Standards Codes, along with tougher local rules designed
to keep embers out of new homes and remodels in the City’s Very High Fire
Hazard Severity Zone. Notable changes in the 2025 code include requirements
for the installation of ember resistant vents to prevent embers from entering
attics, enclosed eaves or eaves constructed with ignition-resistant materials,
and the use of noncombustible construction materials for enclosed eaves.
Once the City Council gives final approval, residents will be made aware
through an informational handout at the counter, and through outreach to the
Tribune.

Earthquake Brace + Bolt Program
Registration for the California Residential Mitigation Program’s Earthquake
Brace + Bolt (EBB) Program will open on August 20 through October 1, 2025.
This program offers eligible homeowners a grant of up to $3,000 to be used
toward a code-compliant seismic retrofit. Many insurance companies now
require this seismic retrofit as a condition of coverage. The San Marino zip
code, 91108 is an eligible area for residents to register, and participants are
selected randomly for the program. An EBB seismic retrofit applies only to

  PAGE 66 of 103
 wood-framed, pre-1980 homes with a raised foundation. For more information
visit www.EarthquakeBraceBolt.com.

Significant Incidents
On July 17, 2025 Engine 91 and Battalion 9 responded to a house fire at 3246
Brandon Street in Los Angeles County Engine 5’s jurisdiction. Upon arrival,
E91 was assigned Rapid Intervention Crew (RIC) and utilities management.
The fire was swiftly extinguished and San Marino Firefighters Stewart, Jarboe,
and Engineer Foth were commended for their high level of professionalism at
the incident.

On Thursday, July 31, at 10:35 AM, San Marino Battalion 9 responded to a
multi-family dwelling fire in the City of Monterey Park. The Chief was assigned
to protect exposure buildings and prevent fire from spreading to uninvolved
structures.

On Thursday, August 14, Engine 91 responded to a home on Virginia Road,
where a 20-month-old toddler had locked themselves into a bathroom.
Firefighter Max Kovshilovskiy used a ladder to access the window of the 2nd
story bathroom and successfully reunited the toddler with their mother.

On Friday, August 15, San Marino Battalion 9 was dispatched to a second
alarm high-rise fire in the City of Glendale. The Chief assisted with command
support. The fire started in one of the units on the 16th floor and vented out
to the roof. Firefighters successfully contained the fire to the vent system.

On Sunday, August 17, San Marino Firefighter/Paramedic Tim Chow was
deployed to the Gifford Fire in the Los Padres National Forest as a Situational
Unit Leader. The Situational Unit Leader is responsible for overseeing map
production, and for fire behavior, fire weather, and incident status inputs on
wildland fire incidents. Firefighter Chow was deployed for 14 days before he
was released on September 1. The City of San Marino is reimbursed 110% of
costs by the State of California for mutual aid responses.

On Saturday, August 30, Engine 91 responded to a two-alarm commercial
structure fire in the City of Montebello. Upon E91’s arrival, the building was
fully involved, and a defensive strategy was implemented. E91 was assigned
to relieve personnel operating at the front entrance to the fire. Captain Tsay,
Engineer Foth, Firefighter/Paramedic Fixsen, and Firefighter/Paramedic
Sawyer performed outstanding, demonstrating exceptional performance and
professionalism.

On September 1, Engine 91 and RA91 responded to a medical alarm activated
by an Apple watch fall. Upon arrival, firefighter/paramedics found the doors

inside. Engine 91 forced entry by breaking a pain of glass in the rear door to

Community
On July 23, Fire Chief Mario Rueda took part in the Smarter Living Series,
presenting a seminar titled “Strengthening San Marino Against Storms &
Urban Fires.” Chief Rueda spoke about the City’s response to the fire and the
damage sustained throughout the City. City personnel responded to over 160
calls for service the night of the windstorm, including multiple vegetation fires,
house fires, downed trees, damaged structures, and downed power lines.
Chief Rueda provided tips on how to harden your home for wildfire and how
to schedule a home fire safety inspection with the Fire Department. For more
information on how to protect your home from wildfire visit
www.SanMarinoCA.gov/FirePrevention.

On August 3, the San Marino Fire Department took part in the National Night
Out event at Lacy Park, joining the San Marino Police Department, the
Community Services Department, and local organizations to promote public
safety and build a stronger community. The Fire Department offered free
hands-only CPR instruction to attendees, as well as resources and tips for
preventing common household fire hazards.

In August, the San Marino Fire Department provided support for another
successful San Marino Motor Classic at Lacy Park. On Saturday, August 23,
firefighters inspected tents and temporary structures to ensure they met local
and state fire safety standards. On Sunday, the Fire Department staffed the
utility vehicle, UTV91, with two Firefighter/Paramedics, who conducted
inspections of food truck vendors, monitored the event for potential fire and
life safety hazards, assisted event organizers with safety compliance, and
remained ready to provide emergency medical care if needed.  The
Firefighter/Paramedics along with the American Red Cross responded to
several emergency medical incidents.

Training
Firefighters Kovshilovskiy and Serrano participated in Fire Apparatus
Driver/Operator 1B training at the Alhambra Training Tower. Driver/Operator
1B is a California State Fire Training course required for completion of
probationary requirements and to complete a firefighter’s Class C Firefighter

  PAGE 68 of 103
 Endorsement drivers license. The class is the second in a two-course series
that teaches driving and hydraulic operations for fire apparatus.

On July 31 and August 1, San Marino firefighters participated in a high-rise
Incident Command System Training with the San Gabriel Fire Department and
other surrounding fire departments at the Sheraton Los Angeles San Gabriel
in the City of San Gabriel. The Sheraton Los is a 5-story 288 room hotel on
Valley Boulevard. Firefighters reviewed command and control, water supply,
evacuation, and fire attack. Although San Marino does not have any high-rise
buildings in our city, our neighbors in Pasadena, Alhambra, and San Gabriel
have several of these buildings. High rise buildings possess very specific
hazards and require knowledge and expertise to combat fires, perform
rescues, and manage other emergencies.

On Tuesday, August 12, the San Marino Fire Department hosted fire personnel
from throughout the San Gabriel Valley for emergency incident/command
simulation training. Simulation training provides a virtual scenario in which
Fire Department personnel act out command of an emergency incident such
as structure fires, hazardous materials release incidents, wildland fires, violent
incidents, etc. in real time with video and live dispatch of the event.
Participants are then able to review their response with training staff to
critique and provide areas for improvement. Chief Rueda has stated many
times, “The cost of tuition at the school of experience is too expensive, better
to learn from others!”

parked on the street in front of their residence. Responding officers located a key fob
inside the victim’s vehicle that did not belong to the victim. The victim also reported
fraudulent charges made at Costco. Investigators conducted an area check of the
nearby Costco and obtained video footage from Costco Loss Prevention of the suspect
using the victim’s credit and debit card. Additionally, investigators located the suspect’s
vehicle in the Costco parking lot. The investigators observed the suspect pulling up to
his parked vehicle in a vehicle of a similar make and model. When the investigators
approached the suspect to speak to him, he drove away. The investigators were able to
identify the suspect through Costco flyers and a photo line-up. The suspect has a
criminal record with multiple felony and misdemeanor convictions including identity
theft, drug charges, and weapons charges. Additionally, the suspect is currently on
probation for carjacking. Investigators are working with outside agencies who reported
the suspect’s vehicle to be involved in a robbery case, grand theft, and identity theft in
their respective jurisdictions.

a ping location in Altadena, CA. Investigators conducted surveillance at the location (a

BACKGROUND

Please accept the following as a summary of notable activities that have been
accomplished, are underway or are planned for the balance of this month
through your next regularly scheduled commission meeting.

DISCUSSION

Traffic-Related Updates

· A status list of all areas requested/identified for traffic conditions review and
analysis is included as Attachment 1 to this report.

Projects in or near Construction

· The Lift Station Improvement Project, which will upgrade the City’s 3 sewer
lift stations, began construction in April. The Orlando Lift Station
improvements are now complete, and work has begun on Monterey Lift
Station. Construction is expected to take 200 working days to complete
upgrades at all three lift stations (80 days for Avondale, 50 days for Monterey,
and 70 days for Orlando).

  PAGE 92 of 103
 · On August 11th, CJ Construction, the City’s sidewalk contractor, began work
on the annual citywide sidewalk replacement project. This project replaces
approximately 1 mile of sidewalk in various locations throughout the City, as
well as limited amounts of curb and gutter and driveway approaches.
Additionally, CJ Construction will be replacing substantial amounts of sidewalk
on Mission Street as part of the Mission District Beautification Project, which
will improve pedestrian safety in the area. Work is expected to be complete
by the end of September.

· At its June 27th meeting, the City Council awarded a contract for Phase 2 of
the Lacy Park Playground Replacement. This phase of the project involves the
replacement of the ages 2-5 structure. Construction is anticipated to begin in
October.

· Recently, the City Council approved an award of contract to CT&T Concrete
Paving for the ADA Sidewalk Ramp Project, which is funded by federal
Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) funds. The City has identified
seventeen (17) sidewalk curb ramps that are in poor condition and/or
currently out of compliance with current ADA accessibility standards.
Replacement of these ramps with ADA-compliant design will provide
accessible paths of travel for users. Construction is anticipated to begin in
October.

· In 2024, City Council approved an award of contract for design services for
the first phase of the Alley and Parking Lot Improvement Program to NV5
Consultants. This program seeks to rehabilitate some of the City-owned alleys
and parking lots each year. The first phase of the project includes
rehabilitation of the two City-owned parking lots at the northeast and
northwest corners of the Huntington Dr and San Marino Ave intersection, as
well as the alleys on the north side of Huntington Dr between Ridgeway Rd
and San Marino High School. Construction is expected to begin later this Fall.

Projects in Design/Out-to-Bid

· Dudek Engineers completed the additional scope that was added to their
contract to evaluate alternative storm drain alignments for the Lacy Park
Culvert Replacement project to re-route the storm drain in public streets in
order to help mitigate the project’s impact on Lacy Park. Dudek will be
proceeding with design of the second alternative alignment that was
determined to be feasible.

· Staff are preparing the Request for Proposals (RFP) package to select a
consultant for the design of the next Street Rehabilitation Project.

  PAGE 93 of 103
 Other Activities

· Assisted other City Departments in the event set up and take down for the
San Marino Motor Classic held at Lacy Park. Activities included mowing and
edging of park, trimming of trees and vegetation, set-up of temporary fencing
and signage, and placing street pole banners for the event.
